questions.subtopic: CUDA / Atomic operations — semantics and contention
questions.learningObjective: Reason about CUDA atomic operations: correctness and the performance impact of contention on hot addresses.
questions.stem: Consider two CUDA reduction kernels: (X) each thread does `atomicAdd(&out[0], x[i])` for one element; (Y) each thread block reduces its region locally via shared-memory tree then does one `atomicAdd(&out[0], partial)`. Which statement about their behavior is correct?

options.text: Both kernels are correct; kernel (X) suffers heavy contention because thousands of threads target the same address, serializing at the atomic unit — kernel (Y) reduces this to one atomic per block (potentially 1000x fewer) while giving the same result modulo FP32 non-associativity.
Kernel (X) is incorrect because `atomicAdd` returns the old value at that address, so calling it in a loop without capturing the return breaks the reduction; only (Y) produces the true sum.
Kernel (Y) is unnecessarily complex; on Ampere+ the hardware atomic unit has infinite bandwidth for FP32 `atomicAdd`, so (X) and (Y) have identical throughput.

Kernel (Y) is incorrect because the shared-memory tree reduction requires `__syncwarp()` inside the loop; only `__syncthreads()` at block boundaries would leave lanes with stale values and produce an off-by-one sum.

assumptions: FP32 hardware atomicAdd on sm_80+.
N is large enough that contention matters (>= 1024).

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Attention — naive scaled dot-product vs materialized attention matrix
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the memory-traffic footprint of naive attention and identify the main bottleneck for long sequences.
questions.stem: In a naive scaled-dot-product attention `O = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V` implemented as three separate kernels (compute S = QK^T, materialize P = softmax(S), compute O = PV), Q/K/V/O are FP16 with shape `[B, H, S, D]`. Which statement about memory traffic on A100 is correct?

options.text: Because Q, K, V are FP16, all intermediate tensors including P and S are automatically kept in registers by the CUDA compiler; there is no HBM traffic for the S × S intermediates regardless of S.
The naive path is limited by the D×D dot product's compute cost, not memory; the S×S intermediate is only S*S/32 elements after warp-level reduction and never materialized in HBM.
Attention is compute-bound at all sequence lengths on A100 because FP16 matmul throughput is far higher than HBM bandwidth; the O(S^2) memory issue is a theoretical concern with no practical impact.

For each (batch, head), the naive path allocates and stores the `S × S` intermediate P (and S) in HBM: `2 * S^2 * sizeof(FP16)` bytes per (batch, head). For `S = 8192`, that is ~256 MB per (B,H) — the O(S^2) memory footprint is the dominant cost and grows quadratically with sequence length, making it infeasible for long sequences.

assumptions: Three-kernel naive implementation without tiled online-softmax.
FP16 storage of Q/K/V/O and intermediates.

questions.subtopic: Triton / triton.autotune and configuration search
questions.learningObjective: Understand triton.autotune configurations and their interaction with kernel launch keys.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton autotuned matmul-like kernel below. Which statements about `triton.autotune` are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: `num_warps` and `num_stages` are per-Config launch parameters (warps per program, pipelining stages) that the autotuner selects together with the tile-size constants; they are not free-form Python arguments.
The autotuner runs at compile time only; once the module is loaded, it never re-tunes even if the caller launches with previously-unseen key values.

`triton.autotune` guarantees that the selected config is globally optimal because it exhaustively searches all possible `(BM, BN, BK, num_warps, num_stages)` combinations, not just the user-provided list.

For each distinct combination of the `key` arguments (here `(M, N, K)`), the autotuner measures each config once, caches the best one, and reuses it for subsequent launches with the same key values; new key values trigger a fresh tuning pass.

assumptions: Standard `triton.autotune` semantics as documented.
The kernel is launched with varying (M, N, K) tuples in practice.

questions.subtopic: Shared memory bank conflicts / Matrix transpose
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a shared-memory transpose kernel and identify which access pattern causes a 32-way bank conflict; know the padding-based mitigation.
questions.stem: Consider the following CUDA matrix-transpose kernel using shared memory, launched with `blockDim = (32, 32)` and `gridDim = (N/32, N/32)` on sm_80. Which statement about shared-memory bank conflicts is correct?

options.text: Both the write (W1) and the transposed read (R1) are conflict-free because sm_80 supports 32-way multicast for shared memory across distinct addresses within the same bank, effectively eliminating serialization.
Write (W1) is conflict-free (row stride-1 across banks); transposed read (R1) causes a 32-way bank conflict since all 32 warp lanes hit one bank; padding to `tile[32][33]` breaks the alignment.
The write (W1) causes a 32-way conflict because 32 threads target the same bank while writing a row; the transposed read (R1) is conflict-free because column accesses spread evenly across banks.

Bank conflicts are automatically eliminated by the CUDA compiler via a promotion pass that pads shared-memory arrays whose access patterns match a canonical conflict template, so no source-level change is required for correctness or performance.

assumptions: Default 4-byte shared-memory bank width on sm_80.
The kernel is intended to transpose an N × N matrix with N a multiple of 32.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Synchronization — __syncthreads vs __syncwarp
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish __syncthreads and __syncwarp semantics and identify when each is appropriate.

hardwareContext.architecture: Volta (sm_70) or newer for ITS semantics

questions.stem: Which statement about `__syncthreads()` and `__syncwarp()` in CUDA is correct?

options.text: `__syncthreads()` synchronizes only the warp of the calling thread; `__syncwarp()` synchronizes the entire block.
`__syncthreads()` and `__syncwarp()` are the same operation with different names for portability; the compiler treats them identically.
Neither `__syncthreads()` nor `__syncwarp()` is required on Volta+, because Independent Thread Scheduling automatically ensures memory visibility and lane convergence at every instruction boundary.

`__syncthreads()` is a block-wide barrier synchronizing all threads in a thread block; `__syncwarp(mask)` synchronizes only the specified lanes within a warp. On Volta+ (with Independent Thread Scheduling), explicit `__syncwarp` is often required between warp-shuffle operations that used to be implicitly convergent.

assumptions: CUDA 11+ toolchain and Volta+ or newer target.

questions.subtopic: Triton / Correctness testing and benchmarking discipline
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the discipline of Triton kernel correctness testing and honest benchmark measurement.

requiredFeatures: Triton runtime; torch backend for reference

questions.stem: Which practices are correct for testing and benchmarking a Triton kernel `my_kernel` versus a PyTorch reference on GPU? (Select all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
import torch, triton

# Sketch of a good benchmark harness
# 1) Warmup:
# for _ in range(warmup):
#     y = my_kernel(x); torch.cuda.synchronize()
# 2) Timed loop:
# torch.cuda.synchronize()
# start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True); end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
# start.record()
# for _ in range(iters):
#     y = my_kernel(x)
# end.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
# ms_per_iter = start.elapsed_time(end) / iters
#
# Correctness:
# y_ref = reference(x)   # e.g. torch.softmax, torch.matmul, etc.
# torch.testing.assert_close(y, y_ref, rtol=..., atol=...)

options.text: Timing a single kernel launch (no warmup, no loop) using Python `time.time()` is a reliable measurement because CUDA is deterministic and one launch captures the true cost.

Autotune-cached configs, JIT-compile time, and cudaGraph capture must always be included in the reported per-iteration latency to fairly compare against a native PyTorch op; a well-run benchmark reports first-launch latency as steady-state.

A per-iteration warmup loop followed by a synchronized-timed inner loop with `torch.cuda.Event` (or equivalent) is the standard pattern; sync before start and after end prevents leaking CPU-launch time or leftover async work into the measurement.

Correctness must compare `my_kernel(x)` against a reference implementation with an explicit tolerance (rtol/atol) chosen for the input dtype and the kernel's expected numerical behavior; using `torch.equal` (bitwise) is generally too strict for FP kernels.

assumptions: CUDA kernel launches are asynchronous with respect to the host by default.
Standard Triton / PyTorch benchmarking harness.

questions.subtopic: Triton / tl.make_block_ptr and block pointers
questions.learningObjective: Understand `tl.make_block_ptr` semantics for structured tile access and how it differs from raw pointer arithmetic.
questions.stem: Which statement about `tl.make_block_ptr` in the following Triton kernel is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def read_tile(in_ptr, M, N,
              stride_m, stride_n,
              pid_m, pid_n,
              BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr):
    block_ptr = tl.make_block_ptr(
        base=in_ptr,
        shape=(M, N),
        strides=(stride_m, stride_n),
        offsets=(pid_m * BM, pid_n * BN),
        block_shape=(BM, BN),
        order=(1, 0),        # innermost dim = axis 1
    )
    x = tl.load(block_ptr, boundary_check=(0, 1))
    # ... use x ...

# in_ptr: FP16 row-major [M, N], stride_m=N, stride_n=1
# BM=64, BN=64

options.text: `tl.make_block_ptr` allocates a shared-memory buffer of size `BM*BN*sizeof(fp16)` on entry and copies the tile into it before use; `boundary_check` prevents the shared-memory allocation from overflowing when the tile extends past `[M, N]`.
`boundary_check=(0, 1)` disables masking on both axes (0 means 'no check on axis 0', 1 means 'no check on axis 1'); users who want masking must specify `boundary_check=None`.

`tl.make_block_ptr` builds a structured pointer describing a `[BM, BN]` tile inside an `[M, N]` tensor; `boundary_check=(0, 1)` tells `tl.load` to mask both axes so out-of-range lanes are safely zeroed; `order=(1, 0)` declares axis 1 as the fastest-varying, matching row-major storage.
The `order` argument sets element endianness inside each 16-bit half; `(1, 0)` reverses the byte order to little-endian on load. It has no effect on which dimension is contiguous in memory.

assumptions: Triton block-pointer semantics as documented.
Row-major FP16 tensor with `stride_m = N`, `stride_n = 1`.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / CUDA Graph — capture, instantiation, launch overhead
questions.learningObjective: Understand CUDA Graph's role in reducing per-launch overhead and its capture/instantiation lifecycle.
questions.stem: Which statement about CUDA Graphs is correct?

options.text: A CUDA Graph is a directed acyclic graph of GPU operations (kernels, memcpys, memsets, host callbacks) captured once (via stream capture or explicit API), instantiated to a `cudaGraphExec_t`, and then launched repeatedly with much lower per-launch CPU overhead than individually launching each op — especially valuable for short kernels where launch overhead dominates.
CUDA Graphs improve every kernel's runtime GPU cost by rewriting the kernel body during instantiation; the CPU-side savings are a small side benefit.
A captured graph can be launched only once per instantiation; each subsequent launch requires re-capturing the graph from a fresh stream.
CUDA Graphs are equivalent to CUDA Streams; they are the same mechanism under different names, and mixing the two APIs on the same context is undefined behavior.

assumptions: Standard CUDA Graph API as documented since CUDA 10.

questions.subtopic: Coalesced access / Global-memory strided reads
questions.learningObjective: Identify the impact of a large stride on effective global-memory bandwidth utilization in a warp-wide load.
questions.stem: The Triton kernel below reads FP32 values from `in_ptr` with a compile-time stride and writes them to `out_ptr` (dense). Launch config: BLOCK=256, stride=8, `in` is a contiguous FP32 tensor of length `N*stride`. On sm_80 (A100), which is the primary performance issue for the load?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def strided_load(in_ptr, out_ptr, N, stride: tl.constexpr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < N
    # in has one useful element per `stride` elements; we sample them all.
    x = tl.load(in_ptr + offsets * stride, mask=mask)   # <-- strided load
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK = 256, stride = 8
# `in`  : FP32 contiguous, length = N * stride
# `out` : FP32 contiguous, length = N

options.text: Because `mask` is applied to the load, no memory transactions occur for lanes with `offsets >= N`; the mask also eliminates any coalescing penalty for the strided access among the valid lanes.

The load triggers shared-memory bank conflicts because 32 threads access addresses 32 bytes apart, and sm_80's bank layout is designed for stride-1 accesses; the conflict serializes each warp into 32 transactions.
The performance impact of strided access is negligible when `BLOCK = 256` because Triton automatically inserts asynchronous copies via `cp.async` that hide the stride penalty behind compute overlap.
Consecutive lanes read addresses stride*4 = 32 B apart; each 128 B L1/L2 sector delivers only 4 useful bytes per lane, so effective global BW is ~1/stride of peak (~ 1/8).

assumptions: The pointer arithmetic `in_ptr + offsets * stride` produces a strided address pattern within a warp.
L1/L2 sector granularity is 128 bytes (or an integer multiple thereof) on sm_80.
No unrolling reorders the accesses into a coalesceable form.

questions.subtopic: Triton / tl.constexpr specialization and re-compilation
questions.learningObjective: Understand `tl.constexpr` semantics: which arguments trigger shape specialization and per-value compilation.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton kernel signature below. Which statement about the difference between `N` and `BLOCK` is correct?

options.text: Both `N` and `BLOCK` are runtime scalars; `tl.constexpr` is a type annotation that affects only IDE tooling and has no impact on compilation or specialization.
Both `N` and `BLOCK` trigger re-compilation on every distinct value; Triton has no notion of runtime scalar arguments.
`N` is compile-time (any change re-compiles); `BLOCK` is runtime. The `tl.constexpr` marker on `BLOCK` is a hint that it is *permitted to be runtime-varying* and is optimized as a register value.

`N` is a runtime scalar passed as a kernel argument; changing `N` reuses the same compiled kernel. `BLOCK: tl.constexpr` is a compile-time constant; each distinct `BLOCK` value triggers a fresh kernel compilation and produces a new specialized PTX.

assumptions: Triton JIT specialization behavior as documented.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Constant memory
questions.learningObjective: Understand what CUDA constant memory is, its size limits, and when its broadcast semantics benefit performance.
questions.stem: Which statement about CUDA `__constant__` memory is correct?

options.text: Constant memory is a runtime-mutable scratchpad allocated from global memory; writes are ordered with respect to `__threadfence()` and it is the standard place for per-warp temporary state.
Constant memory is unlimited in size and is always the fastest memory on the GPU; it should be used in preference to shared memory whenever possible.
Constant memory is a per-thread-block private cache holding read-only tensors; each block gets a fresh 64 KB copy that is invalidated between kernel invocations.

`__constant__` memory is a 64 KB per-module region declared at file scope, cached in a dedicated constant cache; when all threads of a warp read the same address, the read is broadcast in a single access — most efficient for warp-uniform accesses (e.g., small lookup tables, per-block scalar parameters).

assumptions: Standard CUDA `__constant__` semantics.

questions.subtopic: Triton / Differential correctness testing under FP non-associativity
questions.learningObjective: Reason about tolerance selection when a Triton kernel's reduction order differs from a reference implementation.
questions.stem: You wrote a Triton FP16-in/FP32-accumulate matmul kernel and compare its FP32 output against `torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())` (also FP32). You observe max absolute error ~5e-3 and max relative error ~1e-3 on random inputs with K=4096. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.codeSnippet:
# a: [M, K] FP16 row-major; b: [K, N] FP16 row-major; K = 4096
# y = my_kernel(a, b)          # Triton kernel: FP16 in, FP32 accum, FP32 out
# y_ref = torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())   # FP32 reference
#
# Observed:
# torch.max(torch.abs(y - y_ref)).item()                              # ~5e-3
# torch.max(torch.abs(y - y_ref) / (torch.abs(y_ref) + 1e-6)).item()  # ~1e-3

options.text: The reference `torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float())` is itself imprecise on GPU because PyTorch uses TF32 by default on Ampere; the observed error is entirely from the reference and the Triton kernel is exact.

The discrepancy indicates a bug in the kernel: FP32 accumulators guarantee bit-identical output to an FP32 reference, so any deviation above the FP32 machine epsilon (~1e-7) implies an incorrect implementation.

The discrepancy is consistent with expected FP16-input matmul precision: FP16 has ~11 mantissa bits (~3 decimal digits), so per-element rounding accumulates over K=4096 reductions. The observed rtol ~1e-3 is a reasonable tolerance for FP16-input GEMM against an FP32-input reference; the kernel is likely correct.

The discrepancy is due to CUDA's non-determinism; the same kernel will produce a different result each run, so absolute tolerance measurement is meaningless and the test should use `torch.testing.assert_close(atol=inf, rtol=inf)` to always pass.

assumptions: FP16 has ~11 mantissa bits (relative machine epsilon ~9.77e-4).
Random inputs with reasonable range; no NaN/inf pathologies.
K = 4096 accumulation length.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / cp.async and asynchronous global-to-shared copies
questions.learningObjective: Understand cp.async: what it does, on which architectures, and how it enables software pipelining of GMEM→SMEM copies with compute.
questions.stem: Which statement about `cp.async` (introduced in Ampere / sm_80) is correct?

options.text: `cp.async` issues an asynchronous copy from global memory directly to shared memory that does not pass through registers; the copy proceeds in the background while the thread continues executing, and the completion is synchronized with `cp.async.commit_group` + `cp.async.wait_group` (or higher-level barriers). This enables software-pipelined GEMM tile loads.
`cp.async` is a synchronous copy that goes through registers just like a normal load-then-store; the 'async' name refers only to being callable inside asynchronous streams.
`cp.async` is a Hopper-only instruction; on Ampere, all GMEM→SMEM copies must go through registers.
`cp.async` copies from shared memory to global memory (the reverse direction) and is used to flush computed tiles back to HBM without blocking.

assumptions: PTX ISA as of CUDA 11+; sm_80+ hardware.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Warp divergence — cost and mitigation
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the performance cost of intra-warp branch divergence and understand which patterns do or do not cause it.
questions.stem: Which statements about intra-warp branch divergence are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: All conditional constructs in CUDA C++ always compile to divergent branches; the compiler never emits predicated instructions, so `?:` in Case D is exactly as slow as the diverging `if/else` in Case A.

Case A causes intra-warp divergence: the warp effectively serializes into two passes (one for lanes 0-15 running `foo`, one for lanes 16-31 running `bar`), so total cost ≈ cost(foo) + cost(bar) for the divergent instructions rather than max of the two.

Case B is not divergent within a warp because the branch condition depends on `blockIdx`, which is uniform across all threads of a block (and hence across each warp); the warp takes one path with no serialization.

Case D (`v = cond ? a : b`) compiled to predicated instructions avoids serialization but may compute both `a` and `b` (each lane keeps the value selected by its predicate), so if `a` and `b` are expensive, predication can be slower than a well-predicted branch.

assumptions: Standard nvcc code generation for control flow.

questions.subtopic: Triton reduction with atomic accumulation
questions.learningObjective: Reason about correctness, determinism, and initialization semantics of a Triton per-block partial dot-product accumulated via tl.atomic_add.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton kernel below computing a global FP32 dot product via per-block partials accumulated with `tl.atomic_add` into a single-element output `out`. Assume `x, y` are FP32 contiguous CUDA tensors of length N, and the caller sets `out` to 0 before launching. Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def dot_prod(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, N, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    partial = tl.sum(x * y, axis=0)
    tl.atomic_add(out_ptr, partial)

# Caller:
#   out.zero_()
#   grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),)
#   dot_prod[grid](x, y, out, N, BLOCK=1024)

options.text: The kernel is correct: final `out[0]` equals the sum of all partials, and `tl.atomic_add` is necessary because programs concurrently accumulate into the same address.
Reduction order across programs is non-deterministic; for FP32 this can yield bitwise-different results across runs due to floating-point non-associativity.
The `mask=mask, other=0.0` combination in the loads ensures tail lanes contribute 0 to `partial` (since 0 * anything = 0), preserving mask semantics through `tl.sum`.

Setting `out` to a non-zero initial value has no effect on correctness because `tl.atomic_add` overwrites the previous value with each incoming partial, so only the last program's contribution determines the final result stored in memory.

assumptions: `out` is FP32 and supports the atomic add operation on the target GPU.
The launch grid covers all elements; no lanes are skipped.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / FlashAttention — tiling and IO-awareness
questions.learningObjective: Understand FlashAttention's core techniques (tiling, online softmax, IO-aware fusion) and what they achieve.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ampere (A100) tested in the paper; later versions target Hopper

questions.stem: The Triton FlashAttention-forward inner loop iterates over K/V tiles for a fixed Q tile, using an online-softmax running (m, l, acc) state. Which statements about the algorithm are correct? (Select all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# Pseudocode outline for one Q-tile Q_i (fp16, shape [BM, D]):
#   m_i = -inf; l_i = 0; acc = zeros((BM, D), fp32)
#   for j in range(0, S, BN):
#       Kj = load_kv_tile(K, j)          # [BN, D]
#       Vj = load_kv_tile(V, j)          # [BN, D]
#       S_ij = tl.dot(Q_i, Kj.T) * scale # [BM, BN], FP32 accum
#       m_new = max(m_i, tl.max(S_ij, axis=1))
#       P_ij = tl.exp(S_ij - m_new[:, None])            # rescaled
#       l_new = l_i * exp(m_i - m_new) + tl.sum(P_ij, axis=1)
#       acc = acc * exp(m_i - m_new)[:, None] + tl.dot(P_ij.to(fp16), Vj)
#       m_i, l_i = m_new, l_new
#   O_i = acc / l_i[:, None]

options.text: FlashAttention approximates the attention output; the paper reports lower accuracy than standard attention on long-context tasks, so it should be avoided when numerical fidelity matters.
FlashAttention v1's speedup over naive attention comes entirely from replacing the softmax with a cheaper approximation (piecewise-linear exp), not from IO-awareness or tiling.

By processing K/V in tiles and rescaling the running `(m, l, acc)` triple via the online-softmax recurrence, FlashAttention avoids ever materializing the [S, S] score matrix in HBM, reducing HBM traffic from O(S^2) to O(S).

The rescale factor `exp(m_i - m_new)` on `acc` is required because `acc` was previously anchored at `m_i`; the update aligns it to the new anchor `m_new` before adding the new tile's contribution, preserving exact algebra.

assumptions: FlashAttention-forward as documented in the original paper (v1).
SMEM sufficient for tiled Q/K/V blocks.

questions.subtopic: Triton GEMM / FP16 inputs, FP32 accumulation
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the FP16-in / FP32-out matmul pattern common in Triton GEMM kernels and why FP32 accumulation is used.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton GEMM inner loop below. Which statements about the `tl.dot` call and accumulator precision are correct? (Select all that apply.)
questions.codeSnippet:
# A, B, C: FP16 row-major; K-loop accumulator = FP32
acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), dtype=tl.float32)
for k in range(0, K, BK):
    a = tl.load(A_block_ptr)          # FP16, [BM, BK]
    b = tl.load(B_block_ptr)          # FP16, [BK, BN]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, out_dtype=tl.float32)   # accumulate in FP32
    A_block_ptr = tl.advance(A_block_ptr, (0, BK))
    B_block_ptr = tl.advance(B_block_ptr, (BK, 0))
c = acc.to(tl.float16)                # cast back to FP16 for storage
tl.store(C_block_ptr, c)

options.text: FP32 accumulation is only necessary in Triton; CUDA's native `wmma`/`mma.sync` APIs are limited to FP16 accumulation and cannot mix input/accumulator precisions on Ampere or Hopper.

FP32 accumulation is used to avoid catastrophic loss of precision when summing many FP16 partials: FP16's ~3-decimal-digit precision cannot faithfully represent large partial sums that arise from long K-dimension reductions.

On Ampere+, `tl.dot(a, b, out_dtype=tl.float32)` with FP16 inputs lowers to Tensor Core MMA instructions (mma.sync) that accept FP16 operands and produce FP32 accumulator lanes natively, matching the hardware's design.

Casting `acc.to(tl.float16)` at the end is guaranteed to produce a bit-identical result to running the entire kernel in FP16 including accumulation, because FP32→FP16 rounding is a no-op when values are within FP16 range.

assumptions: Tensor Core support on the target GPU (sm_70+).
Triton compiler lowers `tl.dot` with mixed dtypes to mma.sync when supported.

questions.subtopic: CUDA GEMM / Shared-memory tiling — tile shape and reuse
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the compute-to-memory ratio of a shared-memory tiled GEMM and identify how tile size affects reuse.
questions.stem: In a shared-memory tiled FP32 GEMM using thread-block tile size `BM × BN × BK` (with A tile `BM × BK` and B tile `BK × BN`), the number of GMEM bytes loaded per output tile and the number of FMA ops per output tile determine the arithmetic intensity. For a `128 × 128 × 32` thread-block tile, which statement is correct?

options.text: Increasing BK from 32 to 64 halves the SMEM footprint per iteration because the A and B tiles get smaller; therefore, larger BK always improves performance.

Each output tile `128 × 128` requires K/BK iterations of the K-loop. Per iteration: load 128*32*4 + 32*128*4 = 32768 B into SMEM; do 128*128*32*2 = 1_048_576 FLOPs. Per-iteration arithmetic intensity ≈ 1_048_576 / 32768 = 32 FLOPs/byte — high enough to become compute-bound on A100 FP32.

The output tile requires 128*128*4 = 64 KB of registers per thread block for accumulator storage, exceeding the register file on A100; the compiler therefore spills registers to global memory, making this tile size unusable in practice.
Because GEMM is memory-bound at every tile size, changing BM/BN/BK cannot alter the arithmetic intensity; the only way to increase FLOPs/byte is to switch to Tensor Cores.

assumptions: FP32, no Tensor Cores; single-precision FLOPs on A100 ~19.5 TFLOPs; HBM ~1.5 TB/s.
One thread block computes one output tile of size 128×128.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / GEMV — row-parallel dot product with warp reduction
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a CUDA GEMV kernel that assigns one warp per row and identify the memory-bandwidth bottleneck.
questions.stem: The CUDA GEMV kernel below computes `y = A @ x` for a row-major FP32 matrix `A` of shape [M, K] and vector `x` of length K. Launch: `gridDim = (M,)`, `blockDim = (32,)` (one warp per row). Which statement about performance on sm_80 is correct?

options.text: GEMV is compute-bound on A100 because each thread performs a fused-multiply-add per iteration, and the multiply-add throughput on Ampere exceeds the memory throughput; therefore, larger K values improve efficiency asymptotically.
Because every warp reads all of `x`, the kernel is bottlenecked by x's shared-memory bank usage; loading `x` into `__shared__` once per block would eliminate the redundant reads.

The kernel is incorrect because `A[row * K + k]` with `k = lane, lane+32, ...` produces non-coalesced accesses on sm_80: consecutive lanes read addresses `K*4` bytes apart, which is bank-conflicted at the L2.

GEMV is memory-bound on A100: each output element reads K FP32 values from A plus K from x for O(K) traffic and does O(K) FLOPs (arithmetic intensity ~0.25 FLOPs/byte for FP32), well below A100's compute:bandwidth balance. The kernel's per-warp stride-32 access on A gives coalesced reads within a warp; x is loaded redundantly by every row's warp.

assumptions: One warp per output row; blockDim=32.
A100 (sm_80) memory subsystem with 128-byte L2 sectors.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / KV Cache access pattern in decode-phase attention
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the memory-access pattern of KV Cache reads during LLM decode-phase attention.
questions.stem: During LLM decoding (one new token per step), the attention kernel loads Q (only 1 token) and reads the full KV Cache. Which statement about the memory-access pattern is correct?

options.text: Decode-phase attention traffic is constant per token regardless of context length; the KV Cache is compressed by the hardware after each step, so HBM reads do not grow.

Decode-phase attention is heavily memory-bound: for each generated token, Q is a single row while K and V (of length S_kv per sequence) must be fully read from HBM. Arithmetic intensity is very low, and per-step HBM traffic scales linearly with S_kv, growing over the sequence.
The KV Cache is fully cached in L2 for any sequence length, so decoding never reads from HBM after the first step; latency is bounded by L2 hit rate.
Decode-phase attention is compute-bound because MMA operations on Q and K/V dominate; the small Q tensor is negligible compared to the compute cost of the matmul.

assumptions: Standard decode-phase attention without approximations.
S_kv exceeds L2 cache capacity for real workloads.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Launch configuration limits
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the fixed hardware limits on grid and block dimensions and identify which configurations are legal.

hardwareContext.architecture: Ampere (sm_80, A100) and generally similar to modern architectures
requiredFeatures: 1024 threads/block max; 65535 grid.y/z max; 2^31 - 1 grid.x max on sm_60+

questions.stem: For a compute-capability 8.0 (A100) GPU, which of the following kernel launch configurations is legal?

options.text: `gridDim = (1000, 1, 1)`, `blockDim = (33, 32, 1)`. Even though `33 * 32 = 1056 > 1024`, the CUDA runtime silently truncates block dimensions to the nearest multiple of 32, so the launch succeeds with `blockDim.x = 32`.
`gridDim = (1, 1, 1)`, `blockDim = (2048, 1, 1)`. This is legal because a single block can span up to 4096 threads on sm_80 as long as no shared memory is used.

`gridDim = (65535, 65535, 65535)`, `blockDim = (32, 32, 1)`. `blockDim.x * blockDim.y * blockDim.z = 1024 ≤ 1024` and all grid dims are within the 65535 (y/z) / 2^31-1 (x) hardware maximum on sm_80; this is a legal launch.
Grid dimensions on Ampere are hard-capped at 65535 across x, y, z; any request larger than 65535 in any dimension is rejected. This is why one-dimensional grids are always the safest choice.

assumptions: sm_80 (A100) launch limits as documented in CUDA guide.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / LayerNorm — welford / two-pass mean-variance
questions.learningObjective: Reason about a two-pass LayerNorm's memory-traffic cost vs a fused single-pass variant.
questions.stem: The Triton LayerNorm kernel below is fused into a single pass per row (mean, variance, and normalization all inside one program). Which statement about this pattern is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
@triton.jit
def layer_norm(x_ptr, out_ptr, gamma_ptr, beta_ptr,
               N: tl.constexpr, eps: tl.constexpr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = cols < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * N + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    mean = tl.sum(x, axis=0) / N
    xc = x - mean
    var = tl.sum(xc * xc, axis=0) / N
    rstd = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)
    g = tl.load(gamma_ptr + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    b = tl.load(beta_ptr  + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    y = xc * rstd * g + b
    tl.store(out_ptr + row * N + cols, y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (M,), one program per row, BLOCK >= N
# x, out : FP32 row-major [M, N]

options.text: Because `1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)` uses `tl.sqrt`, the kernel is guaranteed to produce bit-identical FP32 results across all NVIDIA GPUs regardless of PTX version.

The fused kernel is mathematically incorrect: computing variance as `sum((x - mean)^2) / N` in one program violates the two-pass Welford requirement, and only a Welford accumulator can produce numerically stable variance.

The kernel keeps the entire row in registers/SMEM across the mean and variance reductions and the final normalization, so `x` is loaded from HBM only once per row; a naive multi-pass implementation that re-reads `x` from HBM after computing mean would double the memory traffic for large M.
Storing `gamma` and `beta` in `__constant__` memory would make this Triton kernel faster because Triton natively places small tensors in constant memory when their size is a `tl.constexpr`.

assumptions: N fits in one program's tile; row-parallel design.
FP32 arithmetic.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / mma.sync — matrix operand layout and warp-level cooperation
questions.learningObjective: Understand the warp-cooperative nature of mma.sync and the register-fragment layout it requires.
questions.stem: Which statement about a Tensor Core `mma.sync` instruction (e.g., `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16.row.col.f32.f16.f16.f32`) is correct?

options.text: `mma.sync` reads its operands directly from global memory and writes accumulators back to global memory; register fragments are only used for the FP32 accumulator.
`mma.sync` is a per-thread instruction: each of 32 lanes independently multiplies its 16×8 block by its 8×16 block, so the warp effectively performs 32 independent MMAs per cycle.

`mma.sync` is a warp-cooperative instruction: all 32 threads in a warp jointly execute one MMA, each holding a fragment of the operands and accumulator in registers per a hardware-defined layout; a single thread cannot execute an mma on its own.
`mma.sync` requires operands to reside in shared memory; the compiler automatically issues `ldmatrix` to fetch them and reissues the mma on every register-file eviction to avoid stalls.

assumptions: Ampere+ mma.sync instruction set as documented in PTX ISA.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Occupancy limiters — registers, SMEM, block size
questions.learningObjective: Understand what limits occupancy in practice: registers per thread, shared memory per block, and threads per block.
questions.stem: On A100 (sm_80: 65536 registers/SM, 164 KB SMEM/SM configurable, max 2048 threads/SM, max 32 blocks/SM), a kernel uses 96 registers per thread, 32 KB SMEM per block, and 256 threads per block. Which statement about the resulting occupancy per SM is correct?

options.text: Registers per SM cap: 65536 / (96 * 256) = 2.66 → 2 blocks. SMEM per SM cap: 164 / 32 = 5.12 → 5 blocks. Thread-count cap: 2048 / 256 = 8 blocks. Block-count cap: 32 blocks. The binding constraint is registers → 2 blocks per SM → 512 active threads → 25% occupancy (relative to 2048 threads/SM peak).
Occupancy is limited by SMEM: 164 KB / 32 KB = 5 blocks. Registers and thread count are secondary. Actual occupancy is 5 * 256 / 2048 = 62.5%.
The compiler automatically spills registers to prevent register pressure from limiting occupancy; therefore, the effective occupancy is 100% (8 blocks × 256 threads = 2048).
Occupancy is determined solely by block size: `2048 / 256 = 8` blocks per SM = 100% occupancy; registers and SMEM only affect performance within a block, not occupancy.

assumptions: A100 (sm_80) hardware limits: 65536 regs/SM, 164 KB SMEM/SM (max carveout), 2048 threads/SM, 32 blocks/SM.
One kernel resident type; no concurrent kernels.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Online softmax — tile-wise running max and sum
questions.learningObjective: Understand the online softmax recurrence used to compute softmax in tiles without materializing the full row.
questions.stem: The online-softmax recurrence processes a row of length N in tiles of size B (with T = N/B tiles). Let `(m_t, s_t)` be the running (max, sum-of-exp-with-max-subtracted) after tile t. Which update rule is correct when a new tile `x_new` (of size B) with local max `m_new` and local sum `s_new = sum(exp(x_new - m_new))` arrives?

options.text: `m = max(m_prev, m_new)`; `s = s_prev * exp(m_prev - m) + s_new * exp(m_new - m)`. The old sum is rescaled by `exp(m_prev - m)` (a value in (0, 1]) to reflect the new anchor; the new tile's sum by `exp(m_new - m)`. This is exact algebra: the merged tile is anchored at the new max.
`m = m_prev + m_new` and `s = s_prev + s_new`; the recurrence is a straightforward sum-of-parts because addition is commutative and softmax is scale-invariant.
`m` remains `m_prev` and `s = s_prev + s_new * exp(m_new)`; the running max is never updated after the first tile because subsequent tiles' contributions are absolutely negligible.
The online softmax recurrence works only for FP16 inputs because FP32 overflows before the second rescale; the algorithm is FlashAttention-specific and not applicable to plain softmax kernels.

assumptions: FP32 accumulation with well-behaved input ranges.
Tiles processed in some (order-agnostic) sequence.

questions.subtopic: Triton / tl.load `other` parameter semantics
questions.learningObjective: Reason precisely about the semantics of the `other` argument in `tl.load` and its interaction with masking and downstream reductions.
questions.stem: You want to compute the *maximum* value of an FP32 tensor `x` of length N via a per-block reduction in Triton. Which value should be passed to `other` in `tl.load` at the tail to preserve correctness?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import math

@triton.jit
def block_max(x_ptr, out_ptr, N,
              BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offs = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offs < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offs, mask=mask, other=???)
    m = tl.max(x, axis=0)          # per-block max
    tl.atomic_max(out_ptr, m)      # atomic reduction to a single output

# out is initialized to -inf before launch
# Launch: grid = (cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK = 1024, N arbitrary

options.text: `other=0.0`: matches the identity for `sum`, and Triton reuses the same identity for both `sum` and `max` reductions so it is safe here too.
`other=-float('inf')` (negative infinity): masked-off tail lanes contribute the identity for `max`, so they do not bias the per-block maximum upward or downward.
`other=float('inf')` (positive infinity): filling with the largest float ensures tail lanes never depress the maximum, guaranteeing correctness of a `max` reduction.
`other=x_ptr[0]`: repeating the first element on the tail keeps the domain of `tl.max` closed under the loaded values, avoiding out-of-domain floats like inf/NaN.

assumptions: IEEE-754 FP32 with support for ±inf.
`tl.max` returns the maximum of the input tile.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Persistent kernel pattern
questions.learningObjective: Understand the persistent-kernel pattern: launch a fixed number of blocks equal to SM count and loop internally over work items.

hardwareContext.architecture: Volta+ (persistent pattern common in Ampere/Hopper serving)
requiredFeatures: work stealing via atomicAdd on a global counter

questions.stem: Which statement about the 'persistent kernel' pattern is correct?

options.text: A persistent kernel launches a fixed number of blocks (typically = SM count × blocks-per-SM) and loops internally over work items pulled from a global queue (e.g., via `atomicAdd` on a counter). It avoids repeated kernel launches for many small work items, amortizes tail-effect load imbalance, and gives the kernel authority over scheduling — at the cost of foregoing the CUDA runtime's dynamic block placement.

A persistent kernel launches one block per work item (like a normal kernel) but marks it as `__persistent__` in nvcc so the runtime keeps its context resident between launches for faster subsequent invocations.
A persistent kernel runs forever until the host explicitly terminates it via `cudaKillKernel`; it is used for background monitoring and cannot be used for compute pipelines.
Persistent kernels require Grace-Hopper CPUs to work; on regular GPU-only nodes they behave like ordinary kernels because they rely on CPU-driven persistent state.

assumptions: Standard CUDA runtime; a hardware-atomic-add counter is available.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Race conditions on shared memory
questions.learningObjective: Identify a race condition in a CUDA kernel that writes and reads shared memory without adequate synchronization.
questions.stem: The kernel below is intended to compute `y[tid] = x[tid-1] + x[tid]` (with `y[0] = x[0]`) using shared memory. Identify the correctness issue.

options.text: Without a `__syncthreads()` between the write `smem[tid] = x[tid]` and the read `smem[tid - 1]`, there is a race: thread `tid` may read `smem[tid - 1]` before thread `tid - 1` has written it. The fix is to insert `__syncthreads()` immediately after the shared-memory store.

There is no race because thread `tid` only reads `smem[tid]` and `smem[tid - 1]`; both writes come from thread `tid - 1` and thread `tid`, which are in the same warp for `tid < 32` and therefore execute in lockstep.
The kernel is incorrect because `__shared__ float smem[256]` requires an explicit `__syncthreads()` at kernel entry to initialize the shared memory to zero.
The write `smem[tid] = x[tid]` is atomic per lane, so no synchronization is needed; the CUDA runtime automatically inserts a barrier before any subsequent shared-memory read.

assumptions: blockDim.x = 256 (multi-warp block).
Modern NVIDIA GPU with ITS behavior.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Warp-level reduction using shuffle intrinsics
questions.learningObjective: Reason about a canonical CUDA warp-level reduction using __shfl_down_sync and identify why the shuffle-tree pattern is required.

hardwareContext.architecture: Volta (sm_70) or newer with independent thread scheduling

questions.stem: Consider the following CUDA warp-reduction snippet inside a kernel where every thread of a warp holds a partial value in `val`. Which statement is correct?

options.text: After the loop, lane 0 holds the sum of all 32 lanes' initial values via a log2(32)=5-step shuffle tree; other lanes hold partial sums that may not equal the total, so consumers must read the result only from lane 0 (or broadcast via `__shfl_sync`).
After the loop, every lane holds the full warp sum because `__shfl_down_sync` broadcasts the result to all lanes at each step.

The reduction is incorrect on Volta+ because Independent Thread Scheduling makes lanes potentially diverge; the correct pattern must use `__syncwarp()` between every shuffle to guarantee lane convergence.
`__shfl_down_sync(mask, val, offset)` is a memory operation that reads from shared memory addressed by `offset`; using it for reductions is inefficient compared to atomic operations in shared memory.

assumptions: warpSize=32 on NVIDIA architectures.
All 32 lanes are active (mask=0xffffffff).

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Register spill and local memory
questions.learningObjective: Understand what CUDA 'local memory' actually is and when register spilling occurs.
questions.stem: In CUDA, when nvcc reports register spilling to 'local memory', which statement is correct?

options.text: 'Local memory' in CUDA is per-thread private storage that lives in global memory (backed by L1 / L2 / DRAM), not on-chip; spilled registers therefore incur high-latency accesses through the memory hierarchy, and heavy spilling typically kills performance.
'Local memory' is a small dedicated on-chip cache (~4 KB per thread) that is faster than shared memory; register spills into it are essentially free and do not affect kernel throughput.
'Local memory' is the same physical memory as shared memory; the compiler decides at build time which lanes get 'local' vs 'shared' slots, and spilling only affects certain warps.
Register spilling never happens because nvcc emits a compile error whenever a kernel would exceed the per-thread register budget; kernels only compile when the register file is sufficient.

assumptions: Standard CUDA memory model as documented since CUDA 1.0.

questions.subtopic: Triton RMSNorm / Launch configuration and register pressure
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the register/SMEM footprint of a row-parallel Triton RMSNorm kernel and how BLOCK sizing affects occupancy.

requiredFeatures: shared memory / register file for row-parallel reductions

questions.stem: Consider the Triton row-parallel RMSNorm kernel below launched with `grid = (M,)` (one program per row), BLOCK=4096, N=4096. Which assessment is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def rms_norm(x_ptr, out_ptr, weight_ptr,
             N: tl.constexpr, eps: tl.constexpr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = cols < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * N + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    var = tl.sum(x * x, axis=0) / N
    rstd = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)
    w = tl.load(weight_ptr + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    y = x * rstd * w
    tl.store(out_ptr + row * N + cols, y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (M,), BLOCK = 4096
# x, out : FP32 contiguous, shape [M, N]; weight : FP32 shape [N]; N = 4096

options.text: The kernel is incorrect because `tl.sum(x * x, axis=0)` requires its own explicit `mask` argument to zero out invalid lanes; without it, tail lanes contribute stale register values and bias the computed variance upwards.
Each program handles one row by loading all `N=4096` FP32 elements into registers/SRAM (~16 KB); this constrains occupancy since the full row lives in one program's tile.

With `BLOCK = N = 4096` the mask is always True, so removing `other=0.0` improves performance by roughly 20% by skipping a redundant predicate check that Triton would otherwise emit on every lane of the load.

`1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)` is guaranteed to be lowered to a `rcpsqrt` PTX instruction that produces bit-identical FP32 results across all NVIDIA architectures, since PTX reciprocal-square-root is an IEEE-strict operation.

assumptions: N=4096 fits within one program's tile; larger N would require a two-pass reduction or online-softmax-style algorithm.
FP32 accumulation of `x * x` is used; FP16 inputs would motivate an FP32 upcast.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Prefix scan (Hillis-Steele vs Blelloch)
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish work-inefficient (Hillis-Steele) from work-efficient (Blelloch) parallel prefix-scan algorithms.
questions.stem: Consider the two parallel inclusive-scan patterns below over a warp/block of N=32 threads. Which statement about the two algorithms is correct?

options.text: Hillis-Steele has depth O(log N) but does O(N log N) work; Blelloch has depth O(log N) and does O(N) work. Blelloch is 'work-efficient': asymptotically fewer operations, but its access pattern is more complex and often needs bank-conflict-avoiding padding on shared memory.
Both algorithms have identical work and depth; the choice between them is purely stylistic and yields identical performance on all NVIDIA architectures.
Hillis-Steele produces the correct output only when the reduction operator is commutative; Blelloch works for any operator. This is why Hillis-Steele is deprecated for FP addition (non-associative).
Blelloch has depth O(N/2) and work O(N); it is faster than Hillis-Steele on serial architectures but not on GPUs, where Hillis-Steele's O(N log N) work is preferred.

assumptions: Both algorithms use shared memory with `__syncthreads()`.
N is a power of two.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Softmax — numerical stability (subtract max)
questions.learningObjective: Understand why the numerically stable softmax subtracts the row maximum before exponentiation.
questions.stem: The Triton row-parallel softmax kernel below computes `y[m, :] = softmax(x[m, :])`. Which statement about the design is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def softmax_row(x_ptr, y_ptr, M, N,
                stride_m, stride_n,
                BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = cols < N
    # Load row into registers
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * stride_m + cols * stride_n,
                mask=mask, other=-float('inf'))
    # (1) Subtract row max for stability
    x_max = tl.max(x, axis=0)
    x = x - x_max
    # (2) Exp and sum
    e = tl.exp(x)
    s = tl.sum(e, axis=0)
    y = e / s
    tl.store(y_ptr + row * stride_m + cols * stride_n, y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid=(M,), BLOCK >= N (single-block-per-row)
# x, y: FP32 row-major [M, N]

options.text: Using `other=-float('inf')` for masked lanes causes the max computation to include -inf and biases `x_max` downward, so real softmax kernels must use `other=0.0` and add a separate `_valid_count` normalization step.
Subtracting `x_max` speeds up the kernel by ~2x on Ampere because Triton uses a fast-path `exp` that only runs on inputs in [-1, 0]; without the subtraction, the slow-path is invoked.

Subtracting `x_max` from every element is a mathematical identity for softmax (numerator and denominator both scale by e^{-x_max}); the transform prevents `tl.exp(x)` from overflowing when `x` contains large values (FP32 `exp` overflows around x ≈ 88.7).
The subtraction is required for correctness because `tl.exp` returns undefined values for any input greater than 0; softmax's mathematical definition assumes all inputs are non-positive.

assumptions: FP32 arithmetic on IEEE-754 hardware.
`tl.exp` is the standard IEEE-consistent expf approximation.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Stream, Event, and asynchronous ordering
questions.learningObjective: Understand CUDA stream ordering semantics and how events synchronize across streams.
questions.stem: Which statements about CUDA streams and events are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: All non-default streams block each other by default; concurrent execution across streams requires an explicit `cudaSetStreamPriority(concurrent=true)` call before use.
`cudaEventRecord` is a synchronous host operation that returns only after the event has been observed by the device; it blocks the calling CPU thread.
Kernels launched on the same non-default stream execute in program order; kernels on different streams may execute concurrently subject to resource availability.

`cudaEventRecord(e, s1)` followed by `cudaStreamWaitEvent(s2, e, 0)` makes any subsequent work on `s2` wait until the event fires (i.e., until all work enqueued on `s1` before the record has completed), enabling cross-stream dependencies without blocking the host thread.

assumptions: Standard CUDA runtime semantics as documented.
Default stream = 0 behavior is per-thread or legacy depending on compile flag; question focuses on non-default streams.

questions.subtopic: Tensor Core / dtypes and per-architecture support
questions.learningObjective: Understand which Tensor Core dtypes are supported on which NVIDIA architectures and how throughput scales.
questions.stem: Which statement about Tensor Core dtype support across NVIDIA architectures is correct?

options.text: Tensor Cores support only FP16; other 'Tensor Core dtypes' (BF16, TF32, INT8, FP8) are software emulations built on the FP16 hardware path.
All Tensor Core dtypes (FP16, BF16, TF32, INT8, FP8) have been supported since Volta; the throughput is identical across all NVIDIA architectures for a given dtype.

Tensor Cores were introduced with Volta (sm_70) supporting FP16 with FP16/FP32 accumulate; Turing (sm_75) added INT8/INT4; Ampere (sm_80) added TF32, BF16, and FP64 Tensor Cores; Hopper (sm_90) added FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) and improved throughput. Not every dtype is on every architecture; kernels must be conditionalized on `__CUDA_ARCH__`.
FP8 Tensor Cores exist on every Ampere GPU; Hopper only added higher clock speeds without introducing new numeric formats to the Tensor Core.

assumptions: NVIDIA architecture history through 2025 as documented in whitepapers.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Texture and __ldg (read-only) path
questions.learningObjective: Understand what the texture / read-only cache path provides and when it is beneficial.

hardwareContext.architecture: Kepler and newer (Kepler introduced read-only path; texture cache older)
requiredFeatures: read-only cache / __ldg intrinsic; texture object API

questions.stem: Which statement about the CUDA texture / read-only cache path (accessed via `__ldg`, texture objects, or `__restrict__` const pointers) is correct?

options.text: The texture cache is faster than shared memory for all access patterns; users should therefore always convert `__shared__` allocations to texture-bound arrays for peak performance.

The read-only path routes global-memory loads through a separate cache (historically the texture cache) that is optimized for read-only, spatially-local data; it can improve L1 pressure and bandwidth for read-only inputs (e.g., weight matrices), and is triggered by `__ldg` or by loading through `const T* __restrict__` pointers on Kepler and later.
`__ldg` is a synchronous host-side intrinsic that pre-copies data from device global memory to host DRAM; using it inside a kernel produces undefined behavior.
The read-only path bypasses coherence; using it on data that another kernel wrote in the same stream will always return stale values, so it should only be used for compile-time-constant arrays.

assumptions: Kepler+ architectures where `__ldg` is available.

questions.subtopic: Triton / program_id and 2D launch grid
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a 2D Triton launch grid maps to `tl.program_id(axis=0)` and `axis=1` and how to compute per-program tile bases.
questions.stem: The 2D Triton kernel below copies a row-major FP32 tensor of shape [M, N] with M=2048, N=1024. Launch: `grid = (triton.cdiv(M, BM), triton.cdiv(N, BN))`, `BM=32`, `BN=128`. Which statement about program (pid_m=17, pid_n=3) is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def copy2d(in_ptr, out_ptr, M, N,
           stride_m, stride_n,
           BM: tl.constexpr, BN: tl.constexpr):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    pid_n = tl.program_id(axis=1)
    offs_m = pid_m * BM + tl.arange(0, BM)
    offs_n = pid_n * BN + tl.arange(0, BN)
    mask_m = offs_m < M
    mask_n = offs_n < N
    # Row-major addressing: element (i,j) at stride_m*i + stride_n*j
    ptrs_in  = in_ptr  + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n
    ptrs_out = out_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_m + offs_n[None, :] * stride_n
    mask = mask_m[:, None] & mask_n[None, :]
    x = tl.load(ptrs_in, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    tl.store(ptrs_out, x, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (cdiv(M, BM), cdiv(N, BN)), BM=32, BN=128
# M=2048, N=1024, row-major FP32, stride_m=N=1024, stride_n=1

options.text: Program (17, 3) copies the tile rows `[17*32 .. 17*32+31]` and columns `[3*128 .. 3*128+127]`, i.e., rows 544..575 and columns 384..511; all lanes are in-bounds (since M=2048>575 and N=1024>511), so the mask is uniformly True and no lanes are skipped.
Program (17, 3) copies rows 17..48 and columns 3..130 because `pid_m * BM + arange(0, BM)` is interpreted as `(pid_m + arange)` due to Python operator precedence in the Triton JIT frontend.
Because `stride_n=1`, the pointer expression `offs_n[None, :] * stride_n` degenerates to a scalar; only column 0 is copied for each row in program (17, 3).
The `mask_m[:, None] & mask_n[None, :]` combination produces a 1D mask of length `BM+BN`; Triton then broadcasts it back to 2D during `tl.load`, which is why passing a 2D mask is redundant.

assumptions: Row-major FP32 layout with `stride_m = N`, `stride_n = 1`.
Triton indexing broadcast semantics as documented in the language reference.

questions.subtopic: Triton / Mask and boundary handling
questions.learningObjective: Reason about how Triton's tl.load/tl.store mask semantics handle out-of-bounds lanes at the tail of a block-tiled kernel.
questions.stem: Consider the Triton vector-add kernel below launched with grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK=1024, N=1_000_000, and 1-D contiguous FP32 CUDA inputs `x`, `y`, `out` of length N. Which statement about the last program (pid = 976) is correct?
questions.codeSnippet:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, N, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < N
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)

# Launch: grid = (triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK),), BLOCK = 1024, N = 1_000_000
# For pid = 976: base = 976 * 1024 = 999_424; offsets = 999_424 .. 1_000_447
# Valid lanes: offsets 999_424 .. 999_999 (576 lanes); OOB: 1_000_000 .. 1_000_447 (448 lanes)

options.text: Because `BLOCK` is a `tl.constexpr`, the mask is fully constant-folded at compile time and lanes with `offsets >= N` still incur memory traffic identical to the non-tail programs, so tail masking provides no bandwidth savings.

The last program reads 448 out-of-bounds addresses which produce undefined values, but even without a mask `tl.load` would remain safe because Triton performs implicit bounds checking on every load operation before dereferencing.

The `mask` argument affects only the store; the load always performs 1024 contiguous global-memory transactions and will read past the end of the tensor whenever `pid * BLOCK + BLOCK > N` on the last program.
Tail lanes with `offsets >= N` (448 lanes here) skip the load (using `other=0.0`) and skip the store thanks to `mask`; no OOB access occurs and those lanes are no-ops.

assumptions: The pointers `x_ptr`, `y_ptr`, `out_ptr` correspond to tensors of length exactly N (no padding beyond).
Triton version implements `mask`/`other` as documented in the language reference.

questions.subtopic: CUDA / Warp size, warp scheduling, and SIMT execution
questions.learningObjective: Reason about warp granularity: how threads are grouped into warps and how a warp is scheduled as a single instruction issue unit.
questions.stem: Which statement about NVIDIA warp execution is correct?

options.text: A warp is a group of 32 threads (`warpSize == 32`) that the SM schedules as a single instruction issue unit; all 32 lanes execute the same instruction on their respective data (SIMT), with per-lane predication used when a branch would otherwise diverge.

Warp size is architecture-dependent and has ranged from 16 to 128 across NVIDIA generations; portable kernels should query `blockDim.x % warpSize == 0` at runtime and adapt block dimensions accordingly.

Warps are software-only abstractions imposed by nvcc for readability; the underlying hardware schedules individual threads independently, and warp-level primitives (shuffles, votes) are software emulations.
Threads in a warp are scheduled in a round-robin order at instruction granularity; even for non-divergent code, each thread of the warp takes 32 cycles to complete one instruction.

assumptions: NVIDIA CUDA GPUs (as opposed to hypothetical wave-64 architectures like AMD).

questions.subtopic: CUDA / WMMA C++ API vs mma.sync PTX
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the CUDA C++ WMMA API from raw mma.sync PTX and understand which layer each occupies.
questions.stem: Which statement about `nvcuda::wmma` (CUDA C++ API) vs raw `mma.sync` (PTX) is correct?

options.text: `wmma` is Volta-only; on Ampere+ users must switch to a completely different API called `cuda::mma`, which is unrelated to `nvcuda::wmma`.
`wmma` and `mma.sync` are mutually exclusive: a kernel using `wmma` cannot invoke `mma.sync`, and vice versa; the compiler will reject any mixture.

`nvcuda::wmma` is a higher-level C++ template API (fragment types, load/store/mma functions) that abstracts the fragment layout and typically compiles down to sequences of `mma.sync` and `ldmatrix` PTX; using raw `mma.sync` gives finer control over shape, layout, and fragment reuse, and is the path used by high-performance libraries like CUTLASS.
`mma.sync` PTX exists only for debugging; production kernels are required to use `wmma` because PTX is not guaranteed to be stable across CUDA versions.

assumptions: CUDA 11+ toolchain.
